title: The Mix-Review Template: How a Full Review Is Built
body:
A mix review is built in five moves. One: state the thing being reviewed in one sentence. Two: gather at least three databases that genuinely bear on it, and name their slugs. Three: take one concrete fact from each database, not a general impression. Four: weigh where the sources agree, where they pull apart, and what is still unknown. Five: close with a verdict the evidence actually supports, plus a one-page quick-reference card.

What a mix review is not: it is not praise pasted over a list of features, and it is not a summary of a single database with other slugs sprinkled on top. If removing one cited database would not change the review, that database was decoration, and the review is sent back until every citation carries weight.
demo_output:
1. State the thing in one sentence
2. Gather 3+ bearing databases
3. Take one concrete fact from each
4. Weigh agreement, tension, unknowns
5. Verdict + quick-reference card
Rule: every cited slug must carry weight.

title: Full Review: The Handheld Calculator as a Cultural Object
body:
The handheld calculator, reviewed through equations, computers, chips, and apps, is four things at once, and the review only works because each database contributes something the others cannot. From equations comes the core truth: a calculator is a solved-problem machine, and its value is measured by whether its answers check out by substitution. From computers comes its lineage: the pocket device is a computer that gave up generality for immediacy, one purpose done instantly.

From chips comes the reason it got cheap enough to be ordinary: a single chip carrying the arithmetic meant the device could be mass-produced, dropped, and replaced without ceremony. From apps comes its afterlife: the same arithmetic now lives inside phones, where it is free, invisible, and taken for granted. The verdict: the calculator's triumph was not power but trust — a small machine whose answers a schoolchild could verify, and whose cheapness made that trust universal. What it lost in the move to apps was exactly that visibility: arithmetic you cannot see is arithmetic you stop checking.
demo_output:
equations (answers check out): 9/10
computers (lineage): 8/10
chips (cheap enough to be ordinary): 9/10
apps (invisible afterlife): 6/10
Overall: 8.0 / 10
Verdict: triumph of trust; loss of visibility in apps.

title: Full Review: A Story Travelling from Book to Comic to Game
body:
Follow one story through books, comics, and games and you see what each medium adds and what it charges. The book gives the story its full interior: time to think, to remember, to change slowly. The comic gives it a face and a pace: a page you can reread in seconds, a moment frozen at its peak. The game gives it a consequence: choices that cost something, endings that differ because the player differed.

The review's tension is real. The book's slowness is the comic's waste and the game's delay; the game's interactivity is the book's loss of authorial control. The verdict is not that one medium wins but that a story survives the journey only if its core survives all three translations: if the idea cannot be drawn in a panel and cannot be played as a choice, it was prose decoration, not story structure. That test — book, panel, choice — is the review's practical gift to any writer.
demo_output:
books (interior, slow change): 9/10
comics (face and pace): 8/10
games (consequence): 8/10
Test: a story survives if it works as prose, panel, AND choice.

title: Full Review: The Home Weather Station
body:
A home weather station, reviewed through earth, experiments, apps, and photography, is a small observatory with a honesty problem. From earth comes the science: temperature, pressure, wind, and rain are measurements with units, ranges, and known error, not impressions. From experiments comes the method: a sensor in direct sun is not measuring air temperature, it is measuring its own housing, and placement is half the instrument.

From apps comes the temptation: a pretty graph smooths away the gaps, the dropouts, and the bad readings, and a station that never reports uncertainty is flattering its owner. From photography comes the fix: a dated photograph of the installation, showing siting and exposure, lets any later reader judge the data instead of trusting it. Verdict: a good station is one that reports its doubts alongside its numbers — siting photograph included, gaps shown, not smoothed.
demo_output:
earth (real units, known error): 9/10
experiments (placement is half the instrument): 9/10
apps (graphs hide gaps): 5/10
photography (dated siting photo): 9/10
Verdict: report doubts alongside numbers; show gaps, never smooth them.

title: Full Review: The City Bus Route
body:
A city bus route, reviewed through transportation, earth, apps, and photography, is a promise written in timetables. From transportation comes the design: frequency matters more than speed on short urban trips, because a bus every ten minutes forgives a missed bus and a bus every hour punishes one. From earth comes the terrain: hills, weather, and river crossings decide where the route can actually go, whatever the map wishes.

From apps comes the live layer: real-time arrival data turns waiting from anxiety into planning, but only where the feed is honest about delays instead of silently re-forecasting them away. From photography comes the ground truth: a photograph of a stop shows shelter, lighting, and step-free access that no timetable records. Verdict: judge a route by its worst hour, not its best — the rainy evening frequency, the unlit stop, the missed connection — because that is when the promise is actually tested.
demo_output:
transportation (frequency beats speed): 9/10
earth (terrain decides): 8/10
apps (honest delay feeds): 7/10
photography (stop ground truth): 8/10
Verdict: judge a route by its worst hour, not its best.

title: Full Review: The Cookbook as a Working Tool
body:
A cookbook, reviewed through cookbook, experiments, photography, and apps, succeeds or fails in the kitchen, not on the shelf. From cookbook comes the structure: a recipe is a procedure with quantities, order, and doneness tests, and a vague recipe is a broken program. From experiments comes the standard: the same dish cooked three times should come out the same way, or the recipe has an uncontrolled variable hiding in it.

From photography comes the check: a photograph of each stage — not just the finished dish — lets a cook see whether they are on track before it is too late. From apps comes the risk: scaling a recipe by tapping a multiplier scales the salt and the cooking time together, and time does not scale like salt. Verdict: a great cookbook is a tested program with pictures at the decision points, and its best feature is a recipe that tells you what failure looks like early enough to fix it.
demo_output:
cookbook (recipe as procedure): 9/10
experiments (repeatability): 8/10
photography (stage photos): 9/10
apps (scaling traps): 6/10
Verdict: a great cookbook shows failure early enough to fix.

title: Full Review: Learning an Instrument from Databases Alone
body:
Can a person learn an instrument using only databases? Reviewed through music, experiments, apps, and words, the honest answer is: most of the way, with one gap that matters. From music comes repertoire and structure: pieces, forms, and what good playing sounds like. From experiments comes practice design: short daily sessions beat rare long ones, and recording yourself turns a vague feeling into evidence.

From apps comes the metronome, the tuner, and the slow-downer — genuinely useful tools that replace three separate purchases. From words comes the vocabulary that lets a learner name what is wrong: intonation, articulation, phrasing. The gap is feedback: no database hears you and winces at the right moment. Verdict: databases can carry a learner to competence, but the last mile still wants a listener — even a recorded one, even a peer — because playing is a conversation, and a conversation needs another ear.
demo_output:
music (repertoire and structure): 9/10
experiments (practice design): 9/10
apps (tuner, metronome, slow-downer): 8/10
words (naming what is wrong): 8/10
Gap: feedback. The last mile wants another ear.

title: Full Review: The Small-Town Newspaper Archive
body:
A small-town newspaper archive, reviewed through news, wiki, photography, and books, is a town's memory with dates attached. From news comes the record: council votes, shop openings, school results, obituaries — the small facts that national papers never carry. From wiki comes the context that turns a name in a 1962 issue into a person with a life and a street address in history.

From photography comes the face of it: a parade photograph, a shopfront, a team portrait, each dated, each naming its people where names are known. From books comes the long view: a local history that stitches fifty years of issues into a narrative a newcomer can actually read. Verdict: the archive's value is inverse to its glamour — the duller the item, the more likely it is the only surviving record of it, and the more carefully it should be kept.
demo_output:
news (small facts, dated): 10/10
wiki (context for names): 8/10
photography (dated faces): 9/10
books (long view): 8/10
Verdict: the duller the item, the more likely it is the only record.

title: Quick-Reference Card: The Calculator Card
body:
One-page AI summary for fast lookup. The calculator: a solved-problem machine whose answers are checked by substitution. Boot equations to verify any numerical claim, computers for lineage, chips for why it became cheap, apps for where the arithmetic went. Rule of thumb: if you cannot check the answer by hand, you do not understand the calculation yet — run the check, not just the computation.

Ask the AI: "Check this calculation" with the equation stated plainly; "What chip made this cheap?" for hardware history; "Where did this function move in apps?" for the modern equivalent. Card limit: this card states what the calculator is and how to check it; it does not teach arithmetic, which lives in the equation database itself.

title: Quick-Reference Card: The Patent and Spec Card
body:
One-page AI summary for fast lookup. Patents (patents) are public records of what has been claimed; specs (specs) are original drafts with manufacture notes and runnable demos. Never blur the two: a patent record proves someone claimed something, a spec draft proves its author designed something in filing shape. Boot patents for prior art, specs for a buildable design, and move patent-to-spec when an idea needs both.

Ask the AI: "Find the closest prior art" with the idea stated plainly; "Draft the spec shape" for the filing structure; "What does the demo prove?" to separate a working program from a description of one. Card limit: this card orients; the databases themselves hold the records, and only they count as evidence.

print('Rule: never blur a claim with a design.')

title: Quick-Reference Card: The Story Card
body:
One-page AI summary for fast lookup. A story survives translation when it works in three forms: as prose in books, as panels in comics, and as choices in games. If an idea cannot be drawn in a panel and cannot be played as a choice, it was prose decoration, not story structure. Use the test in that order — prose first, because the interior is where a story is born; panel second, because pace is where it is felt; choice last, because consequence is where it is proved.

Ask the AI: "Panel this scene" for the visual test; "Choice this scene" for the playable test; "What does the character want, in one sentence?" when the story stalls — a story that cannot answer that question has no engine. Card limit: the test judges structure, not taste; a story can pass the test and still not be to your taste, and that is fine.

title: Quick-Reference Card: The Verification Card
body:
One-page AI summary for fast lookup. Every claim that leaves the network should pass three gates: the validity suite (does it check out against existing records?), the citations database (is the public source named?), and the verification database (is the record itself well-formed — unique id, honest count, working link?). A claim that passes all three can be shared; a claim that fails any one goes back for repair, not out for circulation.

Ask the AI: "Check this claim" for validity; "Cite this" for the public source; "Is this record well-formed?" for the verification gates. Card limit: passing the gates means the claim is supported by the network's records, not that it is true in every sense — evidence has limits, and the card says so rather than hiding it.

print('Gate 1: validity-suite (does it check out?)')
print('Gate 2: citations-database (is the source public and named?)')
print('Gate 3: verification-database (unique id, honest count, working link?)')
print('Share only what passes all three.')
